common_name: Blue Horizon Ageratum (Tall AAS-Winning Cut-Flower Ageratum)

planting.note: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost; Blue Horizon is an AAS-winning tall ageratum, growing much taller than typical bedding ageratum, making it useful as a cut flower rather than only a low edging plant.

directions: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade after the last frost. Blue Horizon was an All-America Selections winner recognized for breaking from the typical low, mounding ageratum habit, growing to two and a half feet tall with long, sturdy stems that make it genuinely useful as a cut flower, unlike most ageratum bred only for low bedding and edging use. It produces the same fuzzy, powder-puff clusters of soft lavender-blue flowers over a long summer season, drawing butterflies, and holds up well in arrangements. Deadheading spent flower clusters encourages continued bloom, and the plant tolerates heat well, though consistent moisture keeps it flowering most vigorously.

common_name: Snow Crystals Alyssum (AAS-Winning Large-Flowered White Alyssum)

planting.note: Direct sow or transplant in early spring or fall in well-drained soil in full sun to light partial shade; Snow Crystals is an AAS-winning alyssum with larger individual flowers and a more vigorous, mounding habit than older, finer-textured alyssum varieties.

directions: Direct sow or transplant in well-drained, average soil in full sun to light partial shade. Snow Crystals is an All-America Selections-winning alyssum bred for larger individual florets and a more vigorous, denser mounding habit than older, fine-textured alyssum varieties, while retaining the same sweet honey fragrance and nonstop bloom. It forms a low, spreading carpet of small white flowers, excellent for edging, rock gardens, and filling gaps between pavers, and performs best in cool spring and fall weather, often slowing or fading in the peak heat of a Gulf South summer. Shearing the plant back by about half if it becomes leggy or stops flowering in summer heat encourages a fresh flush of bloom as temperatures cool.

common_name: Catalina Torenia (Heat-Tolerant Trailing Wishbone Flower Series)

planting.note: Plant transplants after all frost danger has passed in moist, well-drained soil in partial shade to shade; Catalina is a heat-tolerant, trailing torenia series bred to perform well in hot, humid summer conditions where many shade annuals decline.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade to shade. Catalina torenia produces abundant, snapdragon-like flowers in shades of blue, purple, pink, and yellow, each marked with a distinctive dark throat, on a trailing, spreading plant well suited to hanging baskets, containers, and shaded bedding displays. Unlike older torenia varieties that can struggle and decline in peak summer heat, the Catalina series was specifically bred for improved heat tolerance, keeping up strong bloom through the hottest, most humid part of the Gulf South growing season. It thrives in the same moist, shaded conditions that suit impatiens and begonias, and benefits from regular fertilizing and consistent moisture to sustain its nonstop flowering.

planting.note: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost, surface sowing since the fine seed needs light to germinate; Lime Green produces unusual chartreuse-green, star-shaped flowers that pair well with almost any other flower color and are fragrant in the evening.

directions: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade after all frost danger passes. Lime Green is a favorite flowering tobacco cultivar among garden designers and cut-flower growers for its unusual, muted chartreuse-green, star-shaped flowers, a soft color that blends easily into nearly any planting scheme rather than competing for attention. The tubular flowers open in clusters atop sticky, aromatic foliage and release a noticeable sweet fragrance in the evening, attracting moths and other night-flying pollinators. It blooms over a long summer season with routine deadheading and self-seeds modestly in a favorable site, and tolerates the heat and humidity of a Gulf South summer better than many old-fashioned flowering annuals.

planting.note: Plant transplants after last frost in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Snowstorm is a vigorous, heat-tolerant bacopa series bred to hold up better through summer heat than older bacopa varieties, which often decline once temperatures climb.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade, keeping soil consistently moist since bacopa wilts quickly if allowed to dry out. Snowstorm produces a dense, trailing mound of small, dark green leaves smothered in tiny, pure white, five-petaled flowers nearly all season, making it one of the most popular spiller plants for containers and hanging baskets, especially paired with more upright annuals. It was bred for improved heat tolerance compared to older bacopa selections, which historically struggled and stopped flowering once summer temperatures climbed, though consistent moisture and a partly shaded site in the hottest part of the day still help it perform its best through a Gulf South summer. Regular fertilizing supports its continuous bloom.
